questions.title: OS Constraints and Utilities
questions.question: Consider the statements: (i) Operating system implementation has architectural constraints. (ii) Operating system is a set of utilities. Which of the following is true?
questions.solution: An OS is implemented for a particular architecture, and it is also a set of utilities that simplifies application development. Both are correct.

questions.title: Strict Deadlines
questions.question: Operating systems working on strict deadlines are ___.
questions.solution: A real-time OS operates under strict time constraints (e.g. pacemakers, air traffic control).

questions.title: Hard Real-Time Primary Goal
questions.question: What is/must be the primary goal for a hard real-time operating system?
questions.solution: As per the DPP key, efficiency is the primary goal of a real-time OS, since even a little inefficiency can cause heavy loss.

questions.title: Booting and Uni-programming
questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are correct?
options: During booting, OS is loaded into disk from main memory.
The area of memory where OS is stored is known as the system area.
Uni-programming can load and execute a single program in memory.
Uni-programming suffers from idleness of CPU.
questions.solution: During booting the OS is loaded from disk into main memory, so (a) is wrong. The OS area is the system area, uni-programming runs one program at a time and the CPU idles during its I/O.

questions.title: Throughput
questions.question: Throughput is ___.
options: Total number of programs completed per unit time.
Total number of programs loaded into main memory.
questions.solution: Throughput is the number of programs/processes completed per unit time.

questions.title: Pre-emptive Processes
questions.question: Pre-emptive processes have ___.
questions.solution: Pre-emptive scheduling forcefully deallocates the CPU and gives better response time.

questions.title: Non-preemptive Statements
questions.question: Consider the statements: (i) Non-preemptive processes can lead to starvation. (ii) Non-preemptive processes have good response time. (iii) Non-preemptive processes can release the CPU voluntarily. Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution: Non-preemptive processes can cause starvation and release the CPU voluntarily, but they do not have good response time.

questions.title: Functions of an OS
questions.question: Functions of an operating system include ___.
questions.solution: Resource management, security and controlling system performance are OS functions. Reliability is a goal of an OS, not a function.

questions.title: Kernel Mode Only Operations
questions.question: Which of the following are allowed in kernel mode only?
questions.solution: These are privileged instructions. Reading the system time is non-privileged and can be done in user mode.

questions.title: Mode Bit Switching
questions.question: Which of the following is/are correct?
options: To switch from kernel mode to user mode, the mode bit should be changed to 1.
To switch from kernel mode to user mode, the mode bit should be changed to 0.
To switch from user mode to kernel mode, the mode bit should be changed to 1.
To switch from user mode to kernel mode, the mode bit should be changed to 0.
questions.solution: User mode has mode bit 1 and kernel mode has mode bit 0.

questions.title: Match User and Kernel Mode
questions.question: Match the following. Modes: (i) User mode, (ii) Kernel mode. Properties: 1) Atomic, 2) Mode bit 0, 3) Privileged, 4) Preemptive.
questions.solution: User mode is preemptive and non-privileged with mode bit 1. Kernel mode is atomic, privileged and has mode bit 0.

questions.title: Purpose of System Calls
questions.question: A system call is used to access ___.
questions.solution: System calls provide the interface to the operating system's functionality.

questions.title: Function Execution Mode
questions.question: Consider the statements: (i) Pre-defined functions start executing in kernel mode. (ii) User-defined functions start executing in user mode. Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution: All user-defined and pre-defined (library) functions start executing in user mode, so only (ii) is correct.

questions.title: fork() Output Count
questions.question: Consider the following program: main() { fork(); fork(); fork(); printf("GATE 2023"); return 0; } How many times will GATE 2023 be printed?
questions.solution: n fork() calls create 2^n processes in total. 2^3 = 8 processes each execute the printf.

questions.title: Location of Mode Bit
questions.question: The mode bit is present in ___.
questions.solution: The mode bit is stored in the program status word (PSW) register.

questions.title: Mode at System Boot
questions.question: At system boot time, the hardware starts in ___.
questions.solution: At boot, the hardware starts in kernel mode and then loads the OS.

questions.title: Uni- vs Multi-programming
questions.question: Consider the statements: (i) In uni-programming, the CPU can run only one program at a time. (ii) In multi-programming, the CPU can run multiple programs at a time. Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution: A single CPU runs only one process at a time even in multiprogramming; multiple programs are only kept in memory.

questions.title: Incorrect Multiprogramming Statements
questions.question: Which of the following is/are incorrect?
options: Non-preemptive processes may have forceful deallocation.
Non-preemptive multiprogramming is equivalent to uni-programming.
Multiprogramming is of two types: preemptive and non-preemptive.
questions.solution: Non-preemptive processes never have forceful deallocation, and non-preemptive multiprogramming is not equivalent to uni-programming.

questions.title: fork() System Call
questions.question: The fork system call is converted by the compiler and is also known as a ___.
questions.solution: A system call is a supervisory call, executed as a software interrupt that runs privileged code.

questions.title: fork() Statements
questions.question: Consider the statements: (i) A user program gets blocked when a fork call is executed. (ii) The dispatch table contains information regarding all system calls. (iii) The fork system call can execute non-atomically in the system. Which of the following is/are correct?
questions.solution: As per the DPP key, (i) and (ii) are correct.

questions.title: Mode Change and ISR
questions.question: Which of the following is/are correct?
options: Changing mode from user to kernel needs an interrupt.
Changing mode from kernel to user needs an interrupt.
ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) is responsible for mode shifting (user to kernel).
ISR is responsible for changing the mode from kernel to user.
questions.solution: The switch from user to kernel mode happens through an interrupt/ISR; going back to user mode is done by a normal instruction, not an interrupt.

questions.title: Static and Dynamic Data
questions.question: Consider the statements: (i) Static data have fixed size and memory is allocated during run-time. (ii) Dynamic data have different size and memory is allocated during load-time. Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution: Static data have fixed size and memory is allocated at load time; dynamic data are allocated at run time. Both statements are swapped, so both are incorrect.

questions.title: Program vs Process
questions.question: Match the following. (i) Program, (ii) Process with 1. Active entity, 2. Resides in main memory, 3. Passive entity, 4. Resides in disk.
questions.solution: A program is a passive entity that resides on disk. A process is an active entity that resides in main memory.

questions.title: Program Counter
questions.question: The program counter holds ___.
options: Address of the previously executed instruction.
Address of the currently executing instruction.
Address of the next instruction to be executed.
questions.solution: The PC holds the address of the next instruction to be executed.

questions.title: Definition of Process
questions.question: Consider the statements: (i) A program when utilizing the computer's resources is known as a process. (ii) A program performing an I/O operation is considered a process. Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution: A program that is executing (using resources, including doing I/O) is a process.

questions.title: Process and Program
questions.question: Which of the following is/are correct?
options: A process is an instance of a program.
A program loaded into main memory but not currently running is known as a process.
A program is created from a process.
A process is created from a program.
questions.solution: A process is an instance of a program created from it. A program is not created from a process.

questions.title: Match Operations
questions.question: Match the following: Context switching, Message passing, Degree of multiprogramming, Fork() with 1. Dispatcher, 2. Long term scheduler, 3. Process creation, 4. Inter-process communication.
questions.solution: Context switching → dispatcher; message passing → IPC; degree of multiprogramming → long-term scheduler; fork() → process creation.

questions.title: Code Section
questions.question: The memory area where all instructions of a program are stored is known as ___.
questions.solution: The instructions of a program are stored in the code (text) section.

questions.title: Runtime Stack
questions.question: The runtime stack contains ___ of function calls.
questions.solution: The runtime stack stores activation records (frames) of function calls.

questions.title: Operations on a Process
questions.question: How many of the following operations can be performed on a process? Creation, Dispatch, Execute, Block, Terminate.
questions.solution: All five are valid process operations.

questions.title: Suspended and Blocked Processes
questions.question: Which of the following is/are correct?
options: A suspended process resides in memory.
A blocked process resides in memory.
A suspended process resides on disk.
A blocked process resides on disk.
questions.solution: Blocked processes are in main memory, suspended processes are swapped out to disk.

questions.title: Information in PCB
questions.question: Information stored inside a process control block is known as ___ of the process.
questions.solution: The PCB stores the context of a process.

questions.title: Process Information
questions.question: The information about a process is maintained in ___.
options: A Process Context block implemented using an Array
A Process Control block implemented using a Stack
A Process Context block implemented using a Linked list
A Process Control block implemented using a Doubly Linked list
questions.solution: Process information is kept in the Process Control Block (PCB), typically implemented as a doubly linked list.

questions.title: Processes in a System with One CPU
questions.question: Consider a computer with a CPU and N processes. Which of the following is correct regarding the processes?
options: There can be a maximum of N processes in the block state.
There can be a maximum of N processes in the ready state.
There can be at most 1 process in the running state.
There can be at most N processes in the running state.
questions.solution: Only one process can run on a single CPU, while up to N can be blocked or ready.

questions.title: Dispatch Operation
questions.question: If the "Dispatch" operation is performed on a process, which transition is possible?
questions.solution: Dispatch moves a process from Ready to Running.

questions.title: State Diagram Type
questions.question: The given process state transition diagram (New, Ready, Running, Exit) represents: (the diagram is not reproduced in this file)
questions.solution: As per the DPP key, the diagram represents a uni-programming operating system.

questions.title: States in Main Memory
questions.question: If a process is in main memory, then it can be in ___.
questions.solution: Ready, running and blocked processes reside in main memory; suspended processes are on disk.

questions.title: Suspended from Running
questions.question: If a process is suspended from the running state, it is moved to ___.
options: Suspend ready state in main memory
Suspend ready state in secondary memory
questions.solution: A suspended process resides in secondary memory; from running it goes to suspend ready in secondary memory.

questions.title: Queues on Disk
questions.question: Which of the following scheduling queues are present on the disk?
questions.solution: The suspend queue and the input (job) queue reside on disk. Ready and block queues are in main memory.

questions.title: Multiprogramming-only Transitions
questions.question: Which of the following process state transitions is/are present in a multiprogramming OS but not in a uni-programming OS?
questions.solution: Uni-programming has only New → Ready → Running → Exit; the other transitions appear in multiprogramming.

questions.title: Long-term Scheduler Queue
questions.question: The long-term scheduler operates on the ___.
questions.solution: The long-term scheduler picks processes from the job queue (pool) into main memory.

questions.title: Scheduler Between Disk and Memory
questions.question: Which of the following schedulers works between disk and main memory?
questions.solution: The long-term and medium-term schedulers move processes between disk and main memory.

questions.title: Time Inside CPU
questions.question: The time spent by a process inside the CPU is known as ___.
questions.solution: Burst time is the time a process spends executing on the CPU.

questions.title: Context Switching Agent
questions.question: Context switching is done by ___.
questions.solution: The dispatcher performs the context switch.

questions.title: X + Y*Z
questions.question: Consider a system with 5 CPUs and 20 processes. Suppose X is the maximum number of processes that can be in the running state, Y is the minimum number of processes in the ready state, and Z is the maximum number of processes in the block state. Calculate X + Y*Z.
questions.solution: X = 5 (one per CPU). Y = 0 (all processes can be running or blocked). Z = 20. X + Y × Z = 5 + 0 = 5.

questions.title: Swapping Scheduler
questions.question: Which scheduler plays an important role in "swapping"?
questions.solution: The medium-term scheduler handles swapping.

questions.title: Entry into Ready Queue
questions.question: ___ is the time when a process first enters the ready queue.
questions.solution: The time a process first enters the ready queue is its submission/arrival time.

questions.title: Time in Ready Queue
questions.question: If n is the total time spent by a process from arrival till completion, s is the time spent within the CPU and x is the time spent on I/O, which expression gives the total time the process spent in the ready queue?
questions.solution: Time in ready queue = total time − CPU time − I/O time = n − (s + x).

questions.title: Process Completion State
questions.question: A process can complete its execution from which state?
questions.solution: A process can terminate (normally or abnormally) only from the running state.

questions.title: Average Turnaround Time Formula
questions.question: Consider a system with n processes, s is the time when each process terminates, and t is the time each process arrives in the ready queue. What will be the average time for the n processes to complete their execution?
questions.solution: Time to complete execution is turnaround time = completion time − arrival time = sᵢ − tᵢ. The average is Σ(sᵢ − tᵢ) / n.

questions.title: Number of Schedules
questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are INCORRECT regarding the total number of schedules if the system has n processes?
options: Total number of schedules possible in a non-preemptive system are n.
Total number of schedules possible in a non-preemptive system are n².
Total number of schedules possible in a preemptive system are n².
Total number of schedules possible in a non-preemptive system are n!.
questions.solution: A non-preemptive system has n! possible schedules and a preemptive system has infinitely many. So (a), (b) and (c) are incorrect.

questions.title: Schedule Length plus Idle Time
questions.question: Consider a system with three non-preemptive processes. The first process arrives at time 4 and executes for 12 ms. While the first process is executing, the second process arrives at time 6 with burst time 8 ms, and the third process arrives at time 19 with burst time 8 ms. Assume X is the schedule length of the system and Y is the amount of time the CPU is idle and waiting for processes. Calculate X + Y. (CPU time starts at 0.)
questions.solution: Gantt chart: IDLE (0–4), P1 (4–16), P2 (16–24), P3 (24–32). Schedule length X = 32 − 4 = 28, idle time Y = 4. X + Y = 32.

questions.title: Process State Transitions
questions.question: Which of the following statements are CORRECT regarding the process state transition diagram?
options: A process can move from ready to suspend blocked state.
A blocked process can move to suspend ready state.
A blocked process can move to running state.
A running process can move to blocked state.
questions.solution: A ready process moves to suspend ready (not suspend blocked) and a blocked process cannot go directly to running (it goes to ready). As per the DPP key, (b) and (d) are the correct statements.

questions.title: Average TAT using FCFS
questions.question: Consider the following processes with their arrival times and burst times: P1 (AT 3, BT 4), P2 (AT 5, BT 6), P3 (AT 2, BT 5), P4 (AT 0, BT 3). Calculate the average turnaround time of all the processes scheduled using First Come First Serve (up to two decimal places). Scheduling overhead is negligible.
questions.solution: FCFS order: P4, P3, P1, P2 with completion times 3, 8, 12, 18. TAT = 3, 6, 9, 13. Average = 31/4 = 7.75.

questions.title: Sum of Avg WT and Avg TAT
questions.question: Consider the following processes with their arrival times and burst times: P1 (AT 2, BT 5), P2 (AT 5, BT 4), P3 (AT 4, BT 6), P4 (AT 0, BT 4). Calculate the sum of average waiting time and average turnaround time of all the processes scheduled using First Come First Serve (up to two decimal places). Scheduling overhead is negligible.
questions.solution: FCFS order: P4, P1, P3, P2 with completion times 4, 9, 15, 19. Waiting times 0, 2, 5, 10 (avg 4.25). Turnaround times 4, 7, 11, 14 (avg 9). Sum = 13.25.

questions.title: Schedule Length of 6 Processes
questions.question: Consider a preemptive system with 6 processes. Each process executes for 2 ms and leaves the system, and enters again (in any order) after all other processes have executed their first 2 ms. Each process has a burst time of 5 ms. What will be the total schedule length, assuming no process went into the blocked state?
questions.solution: First round: 6 × 2 = 12 ms. Each process then has 3 ms remaining; executing all 6 takes 6 × 3 = 18 ms. Total = 12 + 18 = 30 ms.

questions.title: SRTF with Context Switch
questions.question: Consider arrival time and execution time for the following processes: P0 (AT 2, BT 5), P1 (AT 7, BT 9), P2 (AT 8, BT 3), P3 (AT 10, BT 4). Assume each context switch requires 1 ms (excluding first and last context switch). Calculate the sum of schedule length, turnaround time of P3, and waiting time of P1 using the SRTF algorithm.
questions.solution: Gantt: IDLE(0–2), P0(2–7), CS, P2(8–11), CS, P3(12–16), CS, P1(17–26). Schedule length = 26 − 2 = 24, TAT of P3 = 6, WT of P1 = 10. Sum = 40.

questions.title: Context Switches and Throughput (SJF)
questions.question: Consider arrival time and burst time for the following processes on a single CPU: P0 (AT 1, BT 4), P1 (AT 6, BT 3), P2 (AT 7, BT 9), P3 (AT 5, BT 5). Assume X is the total number of context switches and Y is the throughput of the system using SJF scheduling. Find X + Y. (Exclude start and end context switching; round off up to 2 decimals.)
questions.solution: SJF order: P0, P3, P1, P2 with idle 0–1 and finishing at 22. Context switches X = 3. Throughput Y = 4 / (22 − 1) = 0.19. X + Y = 3.19.

questions.title: Average TAT using SRTF
questions.question: Consider the following processes with arrival and CPU burst times (ms): P0 (0, 4), P1 (2, 3), P2 (3, 4), P3 (5, 5), P4 (1, 2). What is the average turnaround time for these processes using SRTF? (If burst times match, follow lowest arrival time; round off to 1 decimal.)

questions.title: SJF Job Order
questions.question: Five jobs are waiting to be run. Their expected running times are 12, 5, 7, 3 and "X". Which of the following orders will minimize the average completion time using Shortest Job First (SJF)?
questions.solution: SJF runs shorter jobs first, so the order must be increasing. Option (a) places X second, which is optimal when X is the smallest remaining value (X ≤ 3), giving the minimum average completion time (3 + 6 + 11 + 18 + 30)/5 = 13.6 for X = 3. This is the DPP key.

questions.title: CPU Idle Percentage
questions.question: Consider a preemptive SJF scheduling technique followed by three processes P1, P2, P3. All arrive at t = 0 and their total execution times are 30, 40 and 50 units respectively. Each process spends the first 10% of its execution doing I/O, 80% on CPU and the last 10% doing I/O. What will be the CPU idle percentage to execute all processes? (Assume a uniprocessor, all I/O operations can be overlapped; round off up to 2 decimals.)

questions.title: Throughput using FCFS
questions.question: Consider the following processes: P0 (AT 3, BT 2), P1 (6, 3), P2 (12, 3), P3 (5, 2), P4 (25, 4). What is the throughput using FCFS, where scheduling overhead requires 2 units (excluding first and last context switch)?
questions.solution: Schedule runs from time 3 to 31 (length 28) including idle time and context switches. Throughput = 5 / 28 ≈ 0.17.

questions.title: Match Scheduling Algorithms
questions.question: Match List I with List II. List I: (i) SJF, (ii) SRTF, (iii) FCFS. List II: 1. Preemptive, 2. Non-Preemptive, 3. Starvation. Select the correct answer(s) using the code below.
questions.solution: SJF is non-preemptive and has starvation; SRTF is preemptive and has starvation; FCFS is non-preemptive with no starvation. So (b), (c) and (d) are valid matches.

questions.title: SJF and SRTF Statements
questions.question: Consider the following statements: (i) SJF is the most optimal algorithm among all other scheduling algorithms. (ii) SRTF is practically non-implementable because it is pre-emptive in nature. (iii) SJF is practically implementable because of its non-preemptive nature. Which of the following is CORRECT?
questions.solution: Only (i) is correct (SJF is optimal). (ii) and (iii) are incorrect, since SJF and SRTF are both hard to implement because burst time cannot be known in advance. No option lists 'only (i)', so the answer is 'None of these'.

questions.title: Non-preemptive SJF Averages
questions.question: Consider the set of processes: A (AT 2, BT 3), B (4, 17), C (2, 4), D (1, 2), E (7, 5). Assume the processes are scheduled using non-preemptive SJF. What are the average turnaround time and average waiting time?
questions.solution: Order: D, A, C, E, B with completion times 3, 6, 10, 15, 32. Avg TAT = (4 + 28 + 8 + 2 + 8)/5 = 10. Avg WT = (1 + 11 + 4 + 0 + 3)/5 = 3.8.

questions.title: Medium-term Scheduler
questions.question: A scheduler that selects partially executed processes from a secondary storage device is called:
questions.solution: The medium-term scheduler does swapping: it brings partially executed (suspended) processes back from secondary storage into memory.

questions.title: Throughput plus Avg WT (SRTF)
questions.question: Consider the following processes: P0 (AT 0, BT 3), P1 (2, 5), P2 (3, 4), P3 (4, 2), P4 (6, 1), P5 (6, 2). What is the sum of throughput of the system and average waiting time if SRTF scheduling is used? (up to 2 decimals)
questions.solution: Completion times: P0 = 3, P1 = 17, P2 = 12, P3 = 6, P4 = 7, P5 = 9. Waiting times 0, 10, 5, 0, 0, 1 → avg 2.66. Throughput = 6/17 = 0.35. Sum = 3.01.

questions.title: CPU Overhead with SRTF
questions.question: Consider the process table: P0 (AT 6, BT 8), P1 (0, 6), P2 (2, 4), P3 (3, 6), P4 (4, 1), P5 (5, 2). Consider a context switching overhead of 1 unit. What is the percentage of CPU overhead activity while using SRTF? Include the context switch to load the first process and save the last process.
questions.solution: Total context switches = 9 and the schedule length = 36. Overhead = 9/36 = 25%.

questions.title: CPU Scheduling Statements
questions.question: Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct in the context of CPU scheduling?
options: SRTF can be used even when the CPU time required by each process is not known a priori.
Implementing preemptive scheduling may need hardware support.
The goal is to only maximize CPU utilization and minimize throughput.
questions.solution: Turnaround time includes waiting time and preemptive scheduling needs a timer (hardware support). SRTF needs known burst times, and the goal is to maximize both CPU utilization and throughput.

questions.title: Average WT using Non-preemptive SJF
questions.question: Consider the following five processes with arrival and burst times (ms): P0 (1, 3), P1 (0, 2), P2 (4, 4), P3 (3, 6), P4 (6, 2). Using non-preemptive SJF, what will be the average waiting time? (up to 1 decimal)
questions.solution: Order: P1, P0, P2, P4, P3 with completion times 2, 5, 9, 11, 17. Waiting times 0, 1, 1, 8, 3 → average 13/5 = 2.6.

questions.title: Degree of Multiprogramming
questions.question: Which of the following schedulers can control the degree of multiprogramming?
questions.solution: The long-term (job) scheduler decides which processes enter memory, so it controls the degree of multiprogramming.

questions.title: HRRN Statements
questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the HRRN scheduling algorithm?
options: It reduces waiting time for longer processes.
HRRN's response ratio can be calculated as (S + W)/S, where S is the service time and W is the waiting time.
HRRN favours jobs with shorter burst time.
questions.solution: HRRN is non-preemptive, so (b) is incorrect. The response ratio (S + W)/S ages longer waiting jobs while favouring short jobs, so (a), (c) and (d) are correct.

questions.title: SJF vs SRTF Comparison
questions.question: Consider the table: P1 (AT 0, BT 7), P2 (2, 4), P3 (4, 1), P4 (5, 4). Schedule the processes using SRTF and SJF, and select the correct option(s).
options: Waiting time P4(SJF) > Waiting time P3(SRTF).
Waiting time P2(SRTF) < Waiting time P1(SJF).
questions.solution: SRTF average TAT = 28/4 = 7 and SJF average TAT = 32/4 = 8, so (a) is true and (c) is false. WT P4 in SJF = 7 > WT P3 in SRTF = 0 (true). WT P2 in SRTF = 1 is not less than WT P1 in SJF = 0.

questions.title: Algorithms Causing Starvation
questions.question: How many of the following scheduling algorithms may cause starvation? First-come-first-serve, Priority, Shortest process next, Shortest remaining time first.
questions.solution: FCFS has no starvation. Priority, Shortest Process Next (SJF) and SRTF can starve long or low-priority processes. Count = 3.

questions.title: LRTF Waiting Time plus Avg TAT
questions.question: Consider the processes: P1 (AT 0, BT 5), P2 (1, 5), P3 (2, 5), P4 (3, 5). Calculate the sum of the waiting time of process P4 and the average turnaround time using LRTF scheduling. (If the burst times of two processes are the same, schedule the one with the higher arrival time.)
questions.solution: Completion times: P1 = 20, P2 = 19, P3 = 18, P4 = 17. TAT = 20, 18, 16, 14 → average 17. Waiting time of P4 = 9. Sum = 26.

questions.title: HRRN: X * Y + Z
questions.question: Consider 5 processes: P0 (AT 0, BT 4), P1 (3, 5), P2 (4, 6), P3 (5, 5), P4 (8, 3). If the CPU scheduling policy is Highest Response Ratio Next, X is the response ratio of the last process scheduled, Y is the average turnaround time, and Z is the average waiting time. Calculate X * Y + Z (up to 1 decimal).
questions.solution: Order: P0, P1, P2, P4, P3. The last process P3 had response ratio X = (10 + 5)/5 = 3. Average TAT Y = 49/5 = 9.8 and average WT Z = 26/5 = 5.2. X·Y + Z = 29.4 + 5.2 = 34.6.

questions.title: Match Scheduling Groups
questions.question: Match the following groups. Group-I: A. FCFS, B. SJF, C. Priority scheduling. Group-II: 1. Used in time sharing system, 2. Used in real time system, 3. Minimum average waiting time, 4. Convoy effect.
questions.solution: FCFS suffers from the convoy effect, SJF gives minimum average waiting time, and priority scheduling is used in real-time systems.

questions.title: SRTF Completion Order
questions.question: Consider three processes P1, P2, P3 with arrival times 0 ms, 5 ms and 8 ms and processing times 15 ms, 12 ms and 5 ms. They are preemptively scheduled on a single CPU using SRTF. In which order are the processes completed?

questions.title: HRRN Average Waiting Time
questions.question: Consider processes: A (AT 0, BT 4), B (2, 1), C (4, 3), D (5, 5), scheduled using Highest Response Ratio Next. The average waiting time of the processes is ___ ms (up to 1 decimal).
questions.solution: Order: A, B, C, D with completion times 4, 5, 8, 13. Waiting times 0, 2, 1, 3. Average = 6/4 = 1.5.

questions.title: Average TAT using SRTF
questions.question: Consider the following table: P1 (AT 0, service time 6), P2 (1, 3), P3 (2, 1), P4 (3, 4). Find the average turnaround time when processes are scheduled with SRTF (up to 2 decimals).

questions.title: SJF, SRTF and FIFO Statements
questions.question: Consider the statements: (i) If all jobs arrive at the same point in time, an SJF and an SRTF scheduler will behave the same. (ii) If all jobs arrive at the same point in time and have identical run lengths, a FIFO and an SJF scheduler will behave the same. Which of the following statements is true?
questions.solution: With equal arrival times SRTF never preempts, so it behaves like SJF. With identical burst times SJF has no shorter job to pick, so it behaves like FIFO. Both are true.

questions.title: Round Robin Average Waiting Time
questions.question: Consider the process table: P1 (AT 1, BT 2), P2 (6, 4), P3 (4, 10), P4 (5, 6). What is the average waiting time using Round Robin with time quantum 2?
questions.solution: Completion times: P1 = 3, P2 = 16, P3 = 24, P4 = 20. Waiting times: 0, 6, 10, 9. Average = 25/4 = 6.25.

questions.title: Best Response Time
questions.question: Which of the following scheduling algorithms is better than the others in terms of response time?
questions.solution: Round Robin gives every process a CPU slice at fixed intervals, which gives the best response time.

questions.title: Completion Order under FCFS and RR2
questions.question: Consider the 3 processes: P1 (AT 0, BT 5), P2 (4, 7), P3 (6, 4). The completion order of the 3 processes under FCFS and RR2 (round robin with quantum 2) is:
options: FCFS: P1, P2, P3; RR2: P1, P2, P3
FCFS: P1, P3, P2; RR2: P1, P3, P2
FCFS: P1, P2, P3; RR2: P1, P3, P2
FCFS: P1, P3, P2; RR2: P1, P2, P3
questions.solution: FCFS completes P1, P2, P3. With RR2, P3 (4 units) finishes before P2 (7 units), so the order is P1, P3, P2.

questions.title: Round Robin with Context Switch
questions.question: Suppose a system has 5 processes A, B, C, D, E, all arrived at time 0 with burst times 4, 5, 7, 2, 5. The time slice is 2 units and each context switch requires 1 unit (excluding first and last context switch). Which of the following statements is correct?
options: At time 25, Process B is running on the system.
Process E finishes execution at time 31.
Process B finishes its execution before process E.
questions.solution: At time 25 process E is running, E finishes at time 33, and overhead = 12/35 = 34.2%. Process B finishes at time 28, before E at 33, so only (d) is correct.

questions.title: Large Time Quantum in RR
questions.question: In the Round Robin scheduling policy, if the time quantum used is more than the maximum time required to execute any process, then the policy will:
questions.solution: If the quantum exceeds every burst time, each process runs to completion in its turn, so RR degenerates to FCFS.

questions.title: Equal Treatment of Processes
questions.question: Which of the following scheduling algorithms treats every process equally?
questions.solution: Round Robin gives every process an equal time slice regardless of burst length.

questions.title: RR and MLFQ Statements
questions.question: Consider the statements: S1: If all jobs have identical run lengths, an RR scheduler provides better average turnaround time than FIFO. S2: With an MLFQ scheduler, high priority jobs have longer time-slices than low priority jobs. Which of the following is true?
questions.solution: With identical run lengths RR is worse than FIFO for turnaround time, and in MLFQ high-priority queues have shorter time slices. Both statements are false.

questions.title: CPU Efficiency in RR
questions.question: Suppose a system uses round-robin scheduling. e is the time needed for a process switch, w is the round-robin time quantum and n is the average time a process needs to run. What will be the CPU efficiency if the time quantum is greater than the average run time (w > n)?
questions.solution: Each process runs for n and then incurs a switch time e, so efficiency = n / (n + e).

questions.title: CPU Utilization with I/O Wait
questions.question: A process spends 20% of its execution time waiting for completion of I/O. If there are 8 processes in memory at once, the CPU utilization is ___ % (assume all I/O operations are overlapped; up to 2 decimal places).
questions.solution: Utilization = 1 − p^n = 1 − 0.2^8 = 0.9999974, i.e. ≈ 100.00% (the printed key shows 1.00).

questions.title: Exponential Average Prediction
questions.question: Considering the exponential average used to predict the next CPU burst, with α = 0.70, τ0 = 30 ms and previous runs (T0, T1, T2, T3) of 10, 12, 15, 20 ms, the predicted value of τ4 is ___ ms (up to 2 decimal places).

questions.title: Single Ready Queue Limitations
questions.question: What are the limitations of a single ready queue?
options: All processes have to use the same scheduling technique.
Lots of searching time is required to select a single process.
In a single ready queue only a single process can reside.
questions.solution: A single ready queue forces one scheduling technique for all processes and needs searching to pick the next process.

questions.title: MLQ Scheduling
questions.question: Which of the following is/are correct regarding MLQ (multi-level queue) scheduling?
options: Some processes may suffer from starvation.
Processes are divided into categories and scheduled on different ready queues.
Multiple scheduling algorithms can be implemented simultaneously.
questions.solution: As per the DPP key, all four statements are correct for MLQ.

questions.title: Process Affected by Others
questions.question: Which process can be affected by other processes executing in the system?
questions.solution: A cooperating process can affect or be affected by other processes; an independent one cannot.

questions.title: Race Condition
questions.question: A race condition:
options: Occurs when two threads enter the critical section at the same time.
Occurs when one thread is in the critical section and another thread cannot access the critical section.
Occurs when two threads access a shared variable at the same time.
questions.solution: A race condition occurs when two threads access a shared variable concurrently and the result depends on the interleaving.

questions.title: Intra-process Communication
questions.question: Intra-process communication is ___.
options: Two processes within the same system sharing resources.
Two entities within the same process communicating with each other.
Two variables of two processes communicating with each other.
questions.solution: Intra-process communication is between entities (threads) inside the same process.

questions.title: Need for Synchronization
questions.question: In IPC, synchronization is required to eliminate ___.
questions.solution: Synchronization eliminates inconsistency, deadlock and data loss. Progress is a requirement, not something to eliminate.

questions.title: User Mode Execution
questions.question: Consider the statements: (i) User mode execution is non-atomic. (ii) A user process can be preempted after completion of any instruction. Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution: User mode is non-atomic and preemptive, so a process can be preempted after any instruction.

questions.title: Shared Variable
questions.question: Consider two processes: P1 { int x; int y; y = x + 1; x + 1; } and P2 { int p; int y; y = p – 1; p – 1; }. What is the shared variable in both processes?
questions.solution: As per the DPP key, y is the variable common to both processes.

questions.title: Critical Section
questions.question: A critical section is ___.
options: Part of the program which does not access a shared resource.
Complex part of the program which cannot be translated by the compiler.
A section that will always cause deadlock.
Part of the program where shared resources are accessed.
questions.solution: A critical section is the part of a program where shared resources are accessed.

questions.title: Critical Section Variables
questions.question: Consider the producer-consumer code: #define N 1000, int Buffer[N], int count = 0; producer: itemp = Produce_item(); while (count == N); Buffer[in] = itemp; in = (in + 1) % N; count = count + 1; consumer: while (count == 0); itemc = Buffer[out]; out = (out + 1) % N; count = count - 1; process_item(itemc). How many variables from the above code belong to the critical section?
questions.solution: The shared variables accessed by both producer and consumer are Buffer and count; in and out are private to each process.

questions.title: Effects of Preemption
questions.question: Preemption during execution can lead to ___.
questions.solution: Preemption in the middle of a shared-variable update can lead to inconsistency, data loss or incorrect results.

questions.title: Conditions for Synchronization Problems
questions.question: Necessary conditions for synchronization problems to occur in an inter-process communication environment are:
questions.solution: Synchronization problems need a critical section, a race condition and preemption.

questions.title: Producer-Consumer Problem
questions.question: The producer-consumer problem has ___.
questions.solution: Producer and consumer cooperate (through the buffer) but compete for the shared variable count, which can lead to inconsistency and data loss.

questions.title: Entry Section
questions.question: The purpose of the "entry section" in a synchronization mechanism is:
options: To allow all processes to access the shared resource concurrently.
To allow one process at a time to enter the critical section.
To indicate the program has started.
questions.solution: The entry section lets only one of the N processes enter the critical section at a time.

questions.title: Critical Section Requirements
questions.question: What are the requirements of the critical section problem?
questions.solution: A solution must satisfy mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.

questions.title: Mutual Exclusion
questions.question: Mutual exclusion is ___.
options: Any number of processes can enter the critical section if it is free.
No process present in the non-CS should block other processes from entering the CS.
No two processes may be simultaneously present in the CS.
questions.solution: Mutual exclusion means no two processes can be in the critical section at the same time.

questions.title: Two Process Code Analysis
questions.question: Consider two processes X and Y with shared variables x and y initialized to 0. Process X: while (true) { x = 1; while (y == 1) { // critical section; x = 0; } }. Process Y: while (true) { y = 1; while (x == 1) { // critical section; x = 0; } }. Which of the given conditions are satisfied by the above code?
questions.solution: Both processes can be inside the critical section at the same time, so mutual exclusion is not satisfied.

questions.title: Bounded Waiting Violated
questions.question: If the bounded waiting condition is not satisfied, it can cause ___.
questions.solution: Without bounded waiting, one process can enter the CS repeatedly while others starve.

questions.title: Incorrect Statements about CS
questions.question: Which of the following is/are incorrect?
options: A process cannot be pre-empted from the CS.
A process can enter the CS without going into the entry section.
A process can complete/leave the CS without going into the exit section.
A process can be preempted from the entry, exit and critical sections.
questions.solution: A process can be preempted anywhere (including the CS), must go through the entry section to enter, and leaves the CS only by completing the exit section.

questions.title: Software Solutions
questions.question: How many of the following are software-type solutions for synchronization? (i) Lock variable, (ii) Monitor, (iii) Peterson's solution, (iv) Semaphore, (v) Test and Set Lock, (vi) Strict alternation, (vii) Swap.
questions.solution: As per the DPP key, the lock variable and Peterson's algorithm are counted as software solutions. Monitor and semaphore are OS-based and TSL and swap are hardware-based.

questions.title: Minimum Value of x
questions.question: Two processes P1 and P2 execute concurrently: P1: for (a = 1; a <= 4; ++a) x = x + 1; P2: for (b = 1; b <= 4; ++b) x = x + 1. 'a' and 'b' are not shared and x is shared, starting at 0. If P1 and P2 execute only once and concurrently, the final minimum possible value of x is ___.
questions.solution: Interleave so that P1 reads 0, P2 runs 3 iterations (x = 3), P1 writes 1, P2 reads 1, P1 runs its remaining 3 iterations (x = 4), P2 writes 2. Minimum = 2. (The printed DPP key shows 4.)

questions.title: TSL Lock Code
questions.question: Consider the program: Bool Lock = False; void Process(int i) { while(1) { <Non-critical section> while (TSL(&Lock) == True); <Critical Section> Lock = False; } }. Which of the following is correct regarding the given code?
options: It guarantees mutual exclusion but not progress.
It guarantees mutual exclusion and progress but not bounded waiting.
It guarantees progress but not mutual exclusion.
It guarantees progress and bounded waiting but not mutual exclusion.
questions.solution: Test-and-Set Lock gives mutual exclusion and progress but does not guarantee bounded waiting.

questions.title: SWAP Instruction
questions.question: Which of the following is/are correct regarding "SWAP"?
options: It is a software-based synchronization mechanism.
It is based on the "Lock Key" mechanism.
questions.solution: SWAP is a hardware-based atomic (privileged) instruction using the lock-key mechanism.

questions.title: Match TSL and SWAP
questions.question: Match the following: 1. TSL, 2. SWAP with (i) Mutual exclusion, (ii) Progress, (iii) Bounded waiting. Which option is correct?
questions.solution: Both TSL and SWAP guarantee mutual exclusion and progress, but not bounded waiting.

questions.title: TSL and SWAP Issues
questions.question: Which of the following is/are correct?
options: TSL has busy waiting and wastes CPU cycles.
SWAP has busy waiting and utilizes CPU cycles efficiently.
questions.solution: Both TSL and SWAP busy-wait (wasting CPU cycles) and both suffer from priority inversion.

questions.title: Solving Priority Inversion
questions.question: The priority inversion problem can be solved by ___.
options: No solution, and priority inversion can cause deadlock
questions.solution: Priority inheritance is the standard solution to priority inversion.

questions.title: Producer with sleep() and wakeup()
questions.question: Consider the producer code using sleep() and wakeup(): itemp = Produce_item(); X; Buffer[in] = itemp; in = (in + 1) % N; count = count + 1; Y. What will be the values of X and Y respectively?
options: X = if (count == 1) sleep(); Y = if (count == N) wakeup(consumer);
X = if (count == N) sleep(); Y = if (count == N − 1) wakeup(consumer);
X = if (count == N) sleep(); Y = if (count == 1) wakeup(consumer);
X = if (count == N) wakeup(consumer); Y = if (count == 1) sleep();
questions.solution: The producer sleeps when the buffer is full (count == N) and wakes the consumer when the buffer goes from empty to one item (count == 1).

questions.title: Semaphore Operations
questions.question: Operations performed on semaphores are ___.
questions.solution: Semaphores support the wait (P) and signal (V) operations.

questions.title: Types of Semaphore
questions.question: Which of the following are the types of semaphore?
questions.solution: The two types are binary and counting semaphores.

questions.title: Hardware Synchronization Solution
questions.question: Choose the hardware type solution for the synchronization problem from the following.
questions.solution: Test-and-set is a hardware instruction. The others are software solutions.

questions.title: Two-process Turn Solution
questions.question: Consider a two-process synchronization solution where both processes X and Y execute: while (turn == 1); C.S.; turn = 1; The shared variable turn is initialized to zero. How many of the following statements about the solution are incorrect? (i) It violates mutual exclusion. (ii) It violates progress. (iii) It violates bounded wait.
questions.solution: As per the DPP key, the number of incorrect statements is 0.

questions.title: Strict Alternation Properties
questions.question: The software solution strict alternation satisfies which of the following?
questions.solution: Strict alternation guarantees mutual exclusion and bounded wait but not progress.

questions.title: Peterson's Algorithm
questions.question: Choose the correct statements regarding Peterson's algorithm.
options: Peterson's algorithm satisfies only mutual exclusion but not progress.
Peterson's algorithm is a solution for 2 processes.
Peterson's algorithm satisfies mutual exclusion, progress and bounded wait.
Peterson's algorithm is a solution for at least 2 processes.
questions.solution: Peterson's algorithm is a two-process solution that satisfies all three conditions.

questions.title: Synchronization Solutions
questions.question: Which of the following is correct regarding solutions to the synchronization problem?
options: Test and set is a 2-process, software based solution.
Lock variable is a 2-process, hardware based solution.
Strict alternation is a 2-process, hardware based solution.
questions.solution: Test-and-set is hardware based and works for n processes; lock variable and strict alternation are software solutions.

questions.title: Test and Set Characteristics
questions.question: Choose the characteristics of the test-and-set synchronization solution.
options: It does not guarantee bounded wait.
questions.solution: TSL ensures mutual exclusion, is deadlock free, but does not guarantee bounded waiting and so may cause starvation.

questions.title: Best Algorithm for n Processes
questions.question: For implementing synchronization for at least 2 processes (satisfying mutual exclusion, progress and bounded wait), which algorithm is best recommended?
questions.solution: As per the DPP key, none of the listed algorithms is recommended, since they are all two-process solutions.

questions.title: OS-based Synchronization
questions.question: Which of the following is/are OS-based synchronization mechanisms?
questions.solution: Sleep/wakeup, wait/signal (semaphores) and monitors are OS/language-level mechanisms, while swap is a hardware instruction. (The printed key lists (a, c, d).)

questions.title: Counting Semaphore Value
questions.question: A counting semaphore S is initialized to 2 and the following sequence of operations is performed: V V V P V P P P V P P V P V V P. What will be the value of S after these operations?
questions.solution: The sequence has 8 V operations and 8 P operations, so S = 2 + 8 − 8 = 2.

questions.title: Readers-Writers Solution
questions.question: Consider the readers-writers solution: Writer: wait(wrt); writing; signal(wrt). Reader: wait(mutex); readcount++; if (readcount == 1) wait(wrt); signal(mutex); reading; wait(mutex); readcount--; if (readcount == 0) signal(wrt); signal(mutex). Which of the following is/are correct?
options: The readers are not starved of access because of the priority of the writers and vice versa.
A writer gets exclusive access, i.e., while a writer is writing no one can write or read.
questions.solution: As per the DPP key, (a), (b) and (c) are correct; deadlock is not possible.

questions.title: Number of V Operations
questions.question: At a particular time the value of a counting semaphore is 9. Then 20 P operations and x V operations are completed on this semaphore. If the final value of the semaphore is 5, x is:

questions.title: Final Value of Semaphore
questions.question: A counting semaphore is initialized to 5. Then 15 P operations and 20 signal operations are performed on S. What is the final value of S?

questions.title: Classical Reader-Writer Conditions
questions.question: Which of the following conditions must be satisfied in the classical reader-writer problem?
options: Only one writer may write a file at a time.
Only one reader may read a file at a time.
If a reader is reading a file, no writer may write to it.
Any number of readers can read at a time.
questions.solution: Many readers can read together, but a writer needs exclusive access.

questions.title: Awakening a Blocked Thread
questions.question: A thread that is blocked on a semaphore is awakened when another thread:
options: Tries to block the same semaphore
Tries to decrement the semaphore value ≤ 0
Tries to increment the semaphore value ≥ 0
questions.solution: A blocked thread is woken by a signal (V) operation, i.e. an increment of the semaphore.

questions.title: Strict Alternation Limitations
questions.question: Strict alternation:
questions.solution: Strict alternation guarantees mutual exclusion and bounded waiting but not progress.

questions.title: Bounded Buffer Problem
questions.question: The bounded buffer problem is also known as the ___.
questions.solution: The bounded buffer problem is the producer-consumer problem.

questions.title: Compulsory Step for Semaphore
questions.question: What is a compulsory step before using a semaphore?
options: Deciding the final value of the semaphore
Defining the number of operations to be performed
questions.solution: A semaphore must be initialized before use.

questions.title: Semaphore Nature
questions.question: Which of the following is correct?
options: Semaphores are atomic in nature and implemented in user mode.
Semaphores are atomic in nature and implemented in kernel mode.
Semaphores are non-atomic in nature and implemented in user mode.
Semaphores are non-atomic in nature and implemented in kernel mode.
questions.solution: Semaphore operations are atomic and are implemented in kernel mode.

questions.title: Negative Semaphore Value
questions.question: If a semaphore's value is "−3", what does the magnitude of the negative value indicate?
questions.solution: A negative value n means n processes are blocked on the semaphore.

questions.title: flag_critical Routine
questions.question: Processes x1 and x2 use flag_critical to achieve mutual exclusion, initialized to FALSE. get_access: if (flag_critical == FALSE) { flag_critical = TRUE; Critical_section(); flag_critical = FALSE; }. Consider the statements: (i) The above routine may lead to deadlock. (ii) It is possible for processes x1 and x2 to access the critical section concurrently.
questions.solution: Both can see flag_critical == FALSE before either sets it, so concurrent access is possible. No hold-and-wait arises, so deadlock is not possible.

questions.title: Boolean Variables P and Q
questions.question: Processes x1 and x2 use shared Boolean variables P and Q (initially false). x1: while (P == Q); <critical section> P = !(Q); x2: while (P != Q); <critical section> P = Q. Select the true statements: (i) Process x2 can go into the critical section just after one entry by x1. (ii) Mutual exclusion is not ensured. (iii) Process x1 can go into the critical section many times without a single entry of x2.
questions.solution: As per the DPP key, only statement (i) is true.

questions.title: Possible Values of Q
questions.question: Two functions Pi and Pj share a variable Q with initial value 3 and execute concurrently: Pi: R = Q * 2; Q = R; Pj: S = Q + 1; Q = S. How many different possible values can Q have at the end of execution of both processes?
questions.solution: Pi then Pj gives 7; Pj then Pi gives 8; interleavings can give 6 (R written last) or 4 (S written last). Distinct values are 4, 6, 7, 8, so 4 values.

questions.title: Match Concurrency Terms
questions.question: Match the following. A. Critical section, B. Synchronization, C. Mutual exclusion with 1. Ensuring that only one process can execute the C.S., 2. Atomic operations are used to ensure co-operation between processes, 3. Section of code that only one process can access at once.
questions.solution: Critical section → section of code accessed by one process at a time (3); synchronization → atomic operations ensure cooperation (2); mutual exclusion → only one process executes the C.S. (1).

questions.title: Blocked Processes on Binary Semaphore
questions.question: Let S be a binary semaphore with S = 1 initially, and assume no blocked processes exist in the system. The following operations are performed on S: 6 P, 8 V, 12 P, 11 V, 19 P. The number of blocked processes after executing these operations is ___.
questions.solution: As per the DPP key, 19 processes remain blocked after the sequence.

questions.title: Deadlock in Dining Philosophers
questions.question: In the dining philosophers problem, deadlock can occur when:
options: Two philosophers pick their left fork and get preempted before picking the right fork.
Two philosophers sitting in front of each other pick their left fork and then their right fork.
Four philosophers are sitting and doing nothing.
All philosophers pick their left fork and are preempted before picking the right fork.
questions.solution: Deadlock occurs when every philosopher holds the left fork and waits for the right fork.

questions.title: Dining Philosophers Code
questions.question: Consider the code (N = 6): void p(int i) { while (1) { T(i); T_f(i); T_f((i + 1) % N); x(i); p_f(i); p_f((i + 1) % N); } } where T is think, T_f is take fork, x is eat, p_f is put fork and i is the philosopher. Which of the following is true about the above code?
options: Has deadlock but does not have starvation.
Does not have deadlock and starvation.
questions.solution: Every philosopher takes the left fork first, so a circular wait can occur (deadlock), and with deadlock the philosophers starve.

questions.title: Independent Instructions
questions.question: How many of the following instructions can run independently? I1: p = q * r; I2: q = p + z; I3: l = m + k; I4: n = a + b; I5: m = z + s.
questions.solution: As per the DPP key, the instructions form three independent groups: (I1, I2), (I3, I5) and I4.

questions.title: Precedence Graph
questions.question: Consider the instructions I1: a = b + c; I2: d = e * f; I3: k = a + d; I4: l = k + m. Which of the following is the correct precedence graph? (a) I1 → I2 → I3 → I4 in a chain. (b) I3 → I1, I3 → I2 and I3 → I4. (c) I1 → I3, I2 → I3 and I3 → I4. (d) I1 → I2, I2 → I3 and I4 → I3.
questions.solution: I3 needs the results of I1 (a) and I2 (d), and I4 needs I3 (k). I1 and I2 are independent. This is graph (c).

questions.title: co-begin / co-end
questions.question: Solve the following code by co-begin and co-end: x = 4; co-begin x = x + 5; x = x + 6; co-end; What could be the possible final value of x?
questions.solution: Sequential execution gives 15. If the update of x = x + 5 is lost, x = 10; if x = x + 6 is lost, x = 9.

questions.title: Busy Waiting
questions.question: Busy waiting is ___.
options: When a process polls on a variable.
When a process periodically checks a variable.
When a process issues an interrupt.
When a process continuously checks a variable.
questions.solution: Busy waiting means a process continuously checks a variable, wasting CPU cycles.

questions.title: Levels in Precedence Graph
questions.question: Consider the concurrent program S1; Parbegin begin S2; S3; end; begin S4; begin S5; S6; end; Parbegin S7; begin S8; S9 end; Parend; end; Parend; S10. How many levels are there in its precedence graph?
questions.solution: As per the DPP key, the precedence graph has 7 levels.

questions.title: Preventing Dining Philosopher Deadlock
questions.question: Which of the following can prevent deadlock in the dining philosophers problem?
options: Allow at most four philosophers to be sitting simultaneously at the table.
Allow a philosopher to pick up chopsticks only if both chopsticks are available (picked up in a critical section).
An odd-numbered philosopher picks up the left chopstick first and then the right, whereas an even-numbered philosopher picks up the right first and then the left.
questions.solution: Each of the three techniques breaks the circular wait, so all can prevent deadlock.

questions.title: Dining Philosophers Problem
questions.question: The dining philosophers problem is ___.
options: A solution to the producer-consumer problem.
An example of a concurrency-control problem.
questions.solution: It is a classical IPC/concurrency-control problem whose solutions use semaphores. It is not a solution to producer-consumer.

questions.title: Concurrency vs Parallelism
questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are correct?
options: Concurrency is about doing multiple things at once.
Concurrency is about dealing with multiple things at once.
Parallelism is about doing multiple things at once.
Parallelism is about dealing with multiple things at once.
questions.solution: Concurrency is dealing with many things at once; parallelism is doing many things at once.

questions.title: Independent Statements
questions.question: Which condition must be satisfied if two statements are concurrent/independent?
options: At least one shared variable should be present.
No shared variable should be present.
The output of one statement should serve as input to the other statement.
The output of one statement should not serve as input to the other statement.
questions.solution: Independent statements have no shared variables and neither's output is the other's input.

questions.title: begin-end Final Values
questions.question: Consider the code: a = 3; b = 4; begin b = a * b; a = a * b; end; (executed concurrently). What could be the possible final values of a and b?
questions.solution: b = a·b gives 12. If a = a·b runs before b is updated, a = 12; if after, a = 3·12 = 36. So a ∈ {12, 36} and b = 12.

questions.title: Largest Initial Semaphore Value
questions.question: Consider a counting semaphore X with the following operations performed: 20P, 6V, 8V, 7P, 12P, 16V. What will be the largest initial value of X to keep 2 processes in the suspended list?
questions.solution: Total P = 39 and total V = 30. Final value = X + 30 − 39 = −2 → X = 7.

questions.title: Concurrent Program Statements
questions.question: Consider the concurrent program: begin S1; S2; Parbegin S3; S4; S5; Parend; S6; end. Which of the following statements is correct about the above program?
options: S1, S2, S3, S4, S5 run sequentially.
questions.solution: S3, S4, S5 are inside Parbegin/Parend so they run concurrently; S1, S2 and S6 are outside, so they run sequentially.

questions.title: Concurrent Statements after S1
questions.question: Consider the concurrent program: S1; Parbegin begin S2; S3; S4; end; S5; S6; begin S7; S8; S9; end; S10; Parend; S11. After S1, how many statements will start concurrently?
questions.solution: The Parbegin block has five concurrent branches: (S2;S3;S4), S5, S6, (S7;S8;S9) and S10.

questions.title: Definition of Deadlock
questions.question: Deadlock is ___.
options: Blocking a process for a defined time
questions.solution: Deadlock is a situation of infinite (indefinite) waiting.

questions.title: Deadlock and Starvation Statements
questions.question: Which of the following statement is/are correct?
questions.solution: As per the DPP key, deadlock is infinite waiting and starvation is indefinite waiting.

questions.title: Starvation
questions.question: A problem encountered when a process is perpetually denied necessary resources for an indefinite time because the resource is currently used by another process is known as ___.
questions.solution: This is starvation (indefinite blocking). Ageing is the technique used to prevent it.

questions.title: Hardware Resource
questions.question: Which of the following is not a hardware resource?
questions.solution: Semaphores and files are software resources. Registers and the CPU are hardware resources.

questions.title: Blocked Forever
questions.question: If a process request is denied by the OS and it is blocked forever, then the process is in ___.
questions.solution: A process whose request is denied and which is blocked forever is in deadlock.

questions.title: Necessary Conditions for Deadlock
questions.question: What are the necessary conditions for deadlock?
questions.solution: The four necessary conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption and circular wait. 'Pre-emption' itself is not a condition.

questions.title: Cycle and Deadlock
questions.question: Consider the statements: (i) A cycle in a single-instance resource graph is a sufficient and necessary condition for deadlock. (ii) A cycle in a multi-instance resource graph is a necessary and sufficient condition for deadlock. Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution: With single instances a cycle is necessary and sufficient. With multiple instances a cycle is necessary but not sufficient.

questions.title: Deadlock Never Occurs
questions.question: In which deadlock handling strategy can deadlock never occur?
questions.solution: In deadlock prevention and deadlock avoidance, the system never enters a deadlock.

questions.title: Maximum Resources to Cause Deadlock
questions.question: Consider a system having n resources shared between four processes P0, P1, P2, P3 with demands of 6, 9, 7 and 14 respectively. What should be the maximum value of n in order to lead the system to deadlock?
questions.solution: Deadlock happens when every process holds one less than its demand: 5 + 8 + 6 + 13 = 32.

questions.title: Safe Sequences
questions.question: Consider the system state: P1 (allocated 2, maximum 7), P2 (allocated 3, maximum 8), P3 (allocated 4, maximum 6). There are 11 resources in total. Which of the following sequences will lead the system to a safe state?
questions.solution: Available = 11 − 9 = 2. Needs: P1 = 5, P2 = 5, P3 = 2. Only P3 can run first. After it finishes, available = 6, and P1 or P2 can then run. So P3 P2 P1 and P3 P1 P2 are safe.

questions.title: Minimum Resources to Avoid Deadlock (5 Processes)
questions.question: Consider a system with five processes A, B, C, D and E. The resource requirements to complete execution of A, B, C, D and E are 7, 6, 8, 12 and 11 respectively. What is the minimum number of resources required to avoid deadlock in such a system?

questions.title: Maximum Resources for Deadlock
questions.question: If a system has 8 processes, each needing a maximum of 4 instances of a resource R, what is the maximum value of R such that the system is in deadlock?
questions.solution: Deadlock occurs when each process holds (4 − 1) = 3 instances: 8 × 3 = 24. With 25 instances there is no deadlock.

questions.title: Abstract View of Memory
questions.question: According to the abstract view of memory, memory is ___.
questions.solution: From the developer's point of view, memory is a linear one-dimensional array of words/locations.

questions.title: Smallest Addressable Unit
questions.question: What is the smallest addressable unit in a memory?
questions.solution: A byte is the smallest addressable unit in memory.

questions.title: Address Bits for 16 Words
questions.question: If there are a total of 16 words in memory and each word has a size of 8 bytes, how many bits of address are required to refer to one word?
questions.solution: Number of address bits = log2(16) = 4.

questions.title: x * y for Memory Sizes
questions.question: Consider the statements: if there is a memory of size 32 KW, the number of bits required to address one word is x. If the number of bits required to address a memory is 18 bits, the memory capacity is y KW. Calculate x * y.

questions.title: Functions of Memory Manager
questions.question: How many of the following are functions of the memory manager? Memory allocation; Protection; Fragmentation; Address Translation; Manage the execution of larger programs in a smaller memory area.
questions.solution: Functions: memory allocation/deallocation, memory protection and address translation. Avoiding fragmentation and running larger programs in smaller memory are goals, not functions.

questions.title: Banker's Algorithm Requests
questions.question: An OS uses the Banker's algorithm for deadlock avoidance. There are three resource types A, B, C allocated to processes P0, P1, P2. Allocation (A,B,C) / Max (A,B,C): P0 (1,1,3) / (7,4,8); P1 (5,6,2) / (7,8,4); P2 (3,2,1) / (4,5,2). 2 units of each resource are still available and the system is in a safe state. Request 1: P0 requests (2, 0, 1). Request 2: P1 requests (2, 0, 2). Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: Request 1 can be granted, Request 2 cannot.
Request 2 can be granted, Request 1 cannot.
Both Request 1 and Request 2 can be granted.
Neither of Request 1 and Request 2 can be granted.
questions.solution: Request 1 leaves Available = (0,2,1) and no process's need is satisfiable, so it is unsafe. Request 2 leaves Available = (0,2,0) and P1 (need 0,2,0) can finish, then P2 and P0 can run. So only Request 2 can be granted.

questions.title: Resource-Request Algorithm
questions.question: A request of any process should be granted iff the resulting state is safe, otherwise it is denied. This is known as ___.
questions.solution: This is the Resource-Request algorithm used in the Banker's algorithm.

questions.title: Deadlock Prevention Schemes
questions.question: Which of the following are deadlock prevention schemes?
options: Each process requests resources either in only increasing order or in only decreasing order.
Whenever a process requests a resource, it does not hold any other resources.
If a process is holding some resources and requests another resource that cannot be immediately allocated to it, all resources being held are pre-empted.
questions.solution: (a) breaks circular wait, (b) breaks hold and wait, (c) allows pre-emption. All are prevention schemes.

questions.title: Deadlock Statements
questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding deadlock?
options: If a system is in an unsafe state, the process may complete its execution without entering a deadlock state.
If a process releases all its resources before requesting a new resource, then deadlock and starvation are both possible.
Deadlock avoidance is less restrictive than deadlock prevention.
In deadlock avoidance, the request for resources is always granted if the resulting state is safe.
questions.solution: An unsafe state need not lead to deadlock. Releasing all resources before a new request removes hold-and-wait, so deadlock is not possible (b is false). Avoidance grants requests whenever the resulting state is safe, so it is less restrictive than prevention.

questions.title: Mutual Exclusion
questions.question: For mutual exclusion to prevail in the system ___.
options: The processor must be a uniprocessor rather than a multiprocessor.
There must be at least one resource in a sharable mode.
At least one resource must be held in a non-sharable mode.
questions.solution: Mutual exclusion requires at least one resource that is held in a non-sharable mode.

questions.title: Drawback of Static Loading
questions.question: The drawback of static loading is ___.
options: Need to load data before execution
questions.solution: Static loading loads all modules, even unused ones, wasting memory.

questions.title: Loading on Demand
questions.question: Loading of modules of the program on demand is known as ___.
questions.solution: Dynamic loading loads a module at run time only when it is needed.

questions.title: Dynamic Link Libraries
questions.question: Dynamic link libraries are ___.
options: Libraries that are linked with the application during loading
Libraries that are linked with the application after compilation
Libraries that are linked with the application before execution
Libraries that are linked with the application at run time on demand
questions.solution: DLLs are linked with the application at run time, on demand.

questions.title: Address Binding Types
questions.question: Which of the following are address binding?
questions.solution: The three types of address binding are compile-time, load-time and dynamic (execution-time) binding.

questions.title: Address Bits for 32 MB
questions.question: Consider a memory with a capacity of 32 MB. How many bits are required to address this memory?

questions.title: Memory for 28 Address Bits
questions.question: Suppose 28 bits are required to address a memory space. What would be the capacity of the memory?

questions.title: Match Memory Size and Address Bits
questions.question: Match each memory capacity N with the number of bits n required to address it. A: 16 MB, B: 32 KB, C: 8 GB, D: 64 KB with (i) 15 bits, (ii) 16 bits, (iii) 24 bits, (iv) 33 bits.

questions.title: Contiguous Allocation Techniques
questions.question: Which of the following are contiguous allocation techniques in memory management?
questions.solution: Contiguous techniques: overlays, fixed/variable partitions and the buddy system. Paging and segmentation are non-contiguous.

questions.title: Overlaying Statements
questions.question: Consider the statements: (i) Overlaying is only possible when a program can be divided into independent modules. (ii) Overlaying is needed when a process is larger than the amount of memory allocated to it. (iii) Overlaying requires special support from the operating system and is performed in kernel mode. Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution: Overlays are implemented by the user and need no special OS support, so (iii) is incorrect.

questions.title: Partitioning Statements
questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: In fixed length partition, each memory partition should be of the same size.
Memory address protection is done with the help of registers.
Free-space management is done using binary bits.
In fixed-length partition, two programs can reside in one partition.
questions.solution: Fixed partitions can have different sizes (a false). Protection uses base and limit registers and a bit map marks partitions as free (0) or used (1). Only one program can reside in a partition (d false).

questions.title: Next Fit and Worst Fit
questions.question: Consider the statements: (i) Next fit may execute faster than first fit. (ii) Worst fit suffers from internal fragmentation. Which of the following statements is CORRECT?
questions.solution: Next fit avoids rescanning from the start so it can be faster than first fit, and worst fit leaves leftover space in the partition (internal fragmentation).

questions.title: Fixed vs Variable Partition
questions.question: Match the following. Types: (i) Fixed partition, (ii) Variable partition. Features: 1. Suffers from external fragmentation, 2. Suffers from internal fragmentation, 3. Flexible degree of multiprogramming, 4. Preferred allocation policy is worst fit, 5. Preferred allocation policy is best fit.
questions.solution: Fixed partition: internal fragmentation, limited multiprogramming, best fit preferred. Variable partition: external fragmentation, flexible multiprogramming, worst fit preferred.

questions.title: Worst Fit Placement
questions.question: Given memory partitions in order: P1: 200 KB, P2: 400 KB, P3: 150 KB, P4: 500 KB. How would the worst fit algorithm place processes (in order) requiring 215 KB, 300 KB, 25 KB, 400 KB? (The space left after filling a partition is not used by any process.)
questions.solution: Worst fit uses the largest available partition: 215 → P4, 300 → P2, 25 → the largest remaining partition, then 400 KB has to wait. The DPP key marks option (c) as correct.

questions.title: Wastage with Best Fit
questions.question: Consider five memory partitions of size 100 KB, 200 KB, 300 KB, 450 KB and 600 KB. The partitions are to be allotted to processes of size 180 KB, 50 KB, 210 KB, 30 KB and 80 KB. Calculate the memory wastage (in KB) using the best-fit algorithm.
questions.solution: Best fit (partition leftovers are not reused): 180 → 200 KB (waste 20), 50 → 100 KB (waste 50), 210 → 300 KB (waste 90), 30 → 450 KB (waste 420), 80 → 600 KB (waste 520). Total = 20 + 50 + 90 + 420 + 520 = 1100 KB.

questions.title: Resolving External Fragmentation
questions.question: The problem of external fragmentation can be resolved by ___.
questions.solution: Compaction and non-contiguous allocation (e.g. paging) resolve external fragmentation. Overlay does not.

questions.title: Unallocated Partitions (Best Fit)
questions.question: Consider a memory system having six partitions 400 K, 200 K, 300 K, 250 K, 100 K and 500 K. There are four processes of size 289 K, 458 K, 200 K, 300 K. What is the total size of unallocated partitions using the best fit allocation policy (in K)?
questions.solution: 289 → 300, 458 → 500, 200 → 200, 300 → 400. Unallocated partitions are 250 K and 100 K, total 350 K.

questions.title: Compaction and Binding
questions.question: Compaction is possible with ___ address binding.
questions.solution: Compaction relocates processes at run time, which is only possible with dynamic (run-time) binding.

questions.title: Most Efficient Placement Algorithm
questions.question: Given five memory partitions of 200 K, 600 K, 300 K, 400 K, 700 K (in order), how would first-fit, best-fit and worst-fit place processes of 312 K, 517 K, 212 K and 526 K (in order)? Which algorithm makes the most efficient use of memory? (Space left after filling a partition is not used by any process.)
questions.solution: First fit and worst fit leave 526 K waiting, while best fit places all four processes (312 → 400, 517 → 600, 212 → 300, 526 → 700).

questions.title: Internal Fragmentation (First Fit)
questions.question: Consider a memory system with five partitions: 200 K, 250 K, 500 K, 600 K and 300 K (in order). Process requests are of size 200 K, 350 K, 30 K, 25 K, 100 K (in order). How much memory space (in K) will remain unused because of internal fragmentation if first-fit allocation is used?

questions.title: Overlay Memory
questions.question: Consider a program in which horizontally connected blocks are independent modules and vertically connected blocks are dependent modules. Block sizes: A 10 KB, B 5 KB, C 3 KB, D 2 KB, E 5 KB, F 10 KB, G 3 KB, H 4 KB, I 6 KB. Which of the following memory spaces is sufficient to execute the program using overlays?
questions.solution: The overlay paths are A-B-E = 20 KB, A-B-F = 25 KB, A-C-G = 16 KB, A-D-H = 16 KB and A-D-I = 18 KB, so at least 25 KB is needed and anything of 25 KB or more is sufficient. The DPP key marks option (c) 50 KB.

questions.title: Allocation Policy Efficiency
questions.question: A computer has 1000 K of main memory. Jobs arrive and finish in the sequence: Job1 needs 100 K arrives, Job2 needs 250 K arrives, Job3 needs 400 K arrives, Job1 finishes, Job4 needs 40 K arrives, Job5 needs 250 K arrives, Job6 needs 60 K arrives. Which of the following allocation policies performs efficiently?
questions.solution: With first fit, Job4 and Job6 reuse the hole left by Job1 and Job5 fits; with next fit Job5 has to wait. So first fit performs better.

questions.title: Logical Address Bits for 256 MB
questions.question: Consider a paging system with a 256 MB logical address space. How many bits of logical address are required for the given LAS?
questions.solution: 256 MB = 2^28 bytes, so 28 bits.

questions.title: Number of Pages
questions.question: Consider a paging system with 12 bits of logical address where each page is of size 2 KB. Calculate the number of pages in this system.
questions.solution: Page offset = 11 bits, so the number of pages = 2^(12 − 11) = 2.

questions.title: LAS, Pages and Page Size
questions.question: Consider a system with 22 bits of logical address and 12 bits of page offset. Calculate the logical address space, the number of pages, and the page size. Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution: LAS = 2^22 B = 4 MB = 4096 KB. Page size = 2^12 = 4 KB, number of pages = 2^10 = 1K.

questions.title: Operation of Paging Hardware
questions.question: Which among the following is not an operation of paging hardware?
questions.solution: Paging hardware performs address translation and protection. Page fault repair is done by the operating system, not the paging hardware.

questions.title: Pages and Frames
questions.question: Consider the statements: S1: In paging, the logical address space is divided into fixed partitions called "pages". S2: In paging, the physical address space is divided into fixed partitions called "frames". Which of the following is correct?
options: Both S1 and S2 are true
Both S1 and S2 are false
questions.solution: Logical memory is divided into pages and physical memory into frames of the same size.

questions.title: Number of Pages in LAS
questions.question: Consider a system with a 32-bit logical address, a page size of 32 KB and a page table entry (PTE) size of 8 bytes. How many pages are there in the logical address space?
questions.solution: Page offset = 15 bits, so pages = 2^(32 − 15) = 2^17.

questions.title: External Fragmentation Scheme
questions.question: Which of the memory allocation schemes suffers from external fragmentation?
questions.solution: Segmentation uses variable-sized segments and therefore suffers from external fragmentation. Paging suffers only from internal fragmentation.

questions.title: Fifty-Percent Rule
questions.question: There are half as many holes as processes. Let S be the average size of a process and xS be the average size of a hole. If there are n processes in the system, the total memory M is estimated using:
questions.solution: With n/2 holes of average size xS, the total memory is M = nS + (n/2)(xS) = nS(1 + x/2).

questions.title: Logical Address Space from Page Table Size
questions.question: A computer system has a physical address of 128 bits and a page size of 32 KB. Each page table entry contains 4 valid and 2 dirty bits along with the translation bits. If the maximum size of the page table of a process is 60 MB, calculate the size of the logical address space supported by the system (in GB).
questions.solution: Frame bits = 128 − 15 = 113. PTE = 113 + 4 + 2 = 119 bits ≈ 15 bytes. Entries = 60 MB / 15 B = 4M = 2^22. LAS = 2^22 × 32 KB = 128 GB.
