questions.title: Levels of Paging
questions.question: Consider a system with a 512 KB page size where each page table entry requires 8 bytes. How many levels of paging are required to map a 30-bit logical address if every page table fits into a single page?
questions.solution: Page offset = 19 bits, so there are 2^11 pages. A page holds 2^19 / 8 = 2^16 entries, which is more than 2^11, so a single level is enough.

questions.title: Page Table Size
questions.question: A computer system implements a 36-bit virtual address. The page size is 64 KB and the size of physical memory is 34 bits. The approximate size of the page table is ___ MB. (Assume memory is byte addressable.)
questions.solution: Pages = 2^(36 − 16) = 2^20. Frames = 2^(34 − 16) = 2^18, so a PTE needs 18 bits ≈ 3 bytes. Page table = 2^20 × 3 B = 3 MB.

questions.title: Maximum Internal Fragmentation
questions.question: If the page size is 4096 bytes in a paging system and a process needs 20 frames, what is the maximum possible internal fragmentation?
questions.solution: Internal fragmentation can be at most one byte less than a page: 4095 bytes (it occurs only in the last page).

questions.title: Logical Address Bits
questions.question: Consider a virtual address space of eight pages of 2048 words each mapped onto a physical memory of 32 frames. How many bits are there in the logical address?
questions.solution: Eight pages need 3 bits and 2048 words need 11 bits of offset: 3 + 11 = 14 bits.

questions.title: Number of Page Table Levels
questions.question: Consider a virtual memory system with physical memory of 8 GB, a page size of 8 KB and a 46-bit virtual address. Assume every page table exactly fits into a single page. If the page table entry size is 4 bytes, how many levels of page tables would be required?
questions.solution: Virtual pages = 2^(46 − 13) = 2^33. A page holds 8 KB / 4 B = 2^11 entries, so each level resolves 11 bits. Levels = ⌈33 / 11⌉ = 3.

questions.title: Count Correct Statements
questions.question: Consider the statements: (i) Overlays are used to increase the size of physical memory. (ii) The size of virtual memory depends on the size of main memory. (iii) Aging is used to keep track of the number of times a page is referenced. How many of the above are correct statements?
questions.solution: All three are incorrect, so the count is 0.

questions.title: Address Bus Size
questions.question: A processor can support a maximum memory of 8 GB, where the memory is word addressable (each word consists of 4 bytes). The size of the address bus of the processor is at least ___ bits.
questions.solution: 8 GB = 2^33 bytes. Words = 2^33 / 4 = 2^31, so 31 address bits.

questions.title: Paging Statements
questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding paging?
options: Paging helps solve the issue of external fragmentation
Page size has no impact on internal fragmentation
Multi-level paging is necessary to support pages of different sizes
questions.solution: Paging removes external fragmentation and the page table adds memory overhead. Page size does affect internal fragmentation, and multi-level paging is not needed for different page sizes.

questions.title: Objective of Hierarchical Paging
questions.question: What is the basic objective of hierarchical paging?
options: Reduce page table size overhead in memory.
questions.solution: Hierarchical (multi-level) paging reduces the memory overhead of a large page table.

questions.title: Page Table Register
questions.question: The page table register should be made of ___.
questions.solution: The page table base register is consulted on every memory access, so it must be built from very high-speed logic.

questions.title: Main Memory Access Time from EMAT
questions.question: Consider a system implementing paging hardware with a TLB. The entire page table and all the pages are in physical memory. The effective memory access time is 400 msec with TLB hit ratio 0.6 and TLB search time 20 msec. The main memory access time is ___ (in msec).

questions.title: EMAT with Two-level Paging
questions.question: Consider a 2-level paging system with TLB support. The TLB access time is 20 ns and the main memory access time is 300 ns. The CPU finds 126 page references in the TLB out of a total of 180 references. What is the effective memory access time?

questions.title: Page Table Size
questions.question: Consider an operating system with a 32-bit virtual address space and 32 MB physical memory. If the page size is 8 KB, what is the approximate size of the page table in MB?
questions.solution: Entries = 2^32 / 2^13 = 2^19. Frames = 2^25 / 2^13 = 2^12, so a PTE needs 12 bits ≈ 2 bytes. Page table = 2^19 × 2 B = 1 MB.

questions.title: EMAT with TLB
questions.question: Consider a system using paging hardware with a TLB. The entire page table and all pages are in physical memory. It takes 30 ms to search the TLB and 110 ms to access physical memory. If the TLB hit ratio is 0.6, the EMAT (in ms) is ___.

questions.title: Demand Paging Average Access Time
questions.question: A demand paging system takes 240 time units to service a page fault and 300 time units to replace a dirty page. The main memory access time is 20 time units. The probability of a page fault is 0.4. In case of a page fault, the probability of the page being dirty is 0.06. The average access time is ___ time units.

questions.title: EMAT with Four-level Paging
questions.question: Consider a 32-bit machine where a four-level paging scheme is used. The TLB hit ratio is 90%, it takes 30 ns to search the TLB and the main memory access time is 100 ns. What is the effective memory access time in nanoseconds?

questions.title: Bits in Page Table Entries
questions.question: A processor uses a 36-bit physical address and 32-bit virtual addresses, with a page frame size of 4 KB. Each page table entry is 4 bytes. A three-level page table is used, where bits 30–31 index the first level, bits 21–29 the second level, bits 12–20 the third level, and bits 0–11 are the offset. How many bits are required for addressing the next-level page table (or page frame) in the entries of the first, second and third level page tables respectively?
questions.solution: A page frame needs 36 − 12 = 24 bits. Number of third-level tables possible = 2^36 / 2^11 = 2^25 and number of second-level tables = 2^25 as well, so the first and second level entries need 25 bits.

questions.title: Fragmentation Statements
questions.question: Consider the statements: (i) Paging never suffers from internal fragmentation. (ii) Segmentation never suffers from external fragmentation. (iii) Segmentation may suffer from internal fragmentation. How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution: Paging may have internal fragmentation but never external fragmentation. Segmentation has no internal fragmentation but may suffer from external fragmentation. All three statements are false, so the count is 0.

questions.title: Segment Table Trap
questions.question: Consider the segment table: Segment 0 (base 5519, length 400), 1 (2500, 15), 2 (100, 500), 3 (1257, 600), 4 (1859, 500). Which of the following 13-bit logical addresses (3-bit segment number, 10-bit offset) will generate a trap addressing error?
questions.solution: (a) segment 0, offset 410 > 400 → trap. (b) segment 1, offset 15 is not less than the length 15 → trap. (c) segment 2, offset 300 < 500 and (d) segment 4, offset 499 < 500 are valid.

questions.title: Implementing Virtual Memory
questions.question: Virtual memory can be implemented using ___.
questions.solution: Virtual memory is implemented through demand paging, which loads pages on demand at run time.

questions.title: Access Time Relation
questions.question: If x is TLB or cache access time, y is main memory access time, and z is page fault service time or disk access time, which of the following relations is correct regarding access time?
questions.solution: Cache/TLB is faster than main memory, which is faster than disk: x < y < z.

questions.title: Limit of Virtual Memory Size
questions.question: The size of virtual memory is limited by ___.
questions.solution: Virtual memory resides on disk, so its size is limited by the disk size (as per the DPP key).

questions.title: Levels of Paging for Single-page Table
questions.question: How many levels of paging are required if it is desired to limit the page table to 1 page, assuming page size = 4 KB, entry size e = 4 B and a 64-bit logical address?
questions.solution: Offset = 12 bits, so 52 bits remain. Each level resolves log2(4 KB / 4 B) = 10 bits. Levels = ⌈52 / 10⌉ = 6.

questions.title: Segment Table Size
questions.question: Consider a system using segmented paging, where a segment is divided into 16K pages each of size 4 KB and the segment table is divided into 8K pages each of size 2 KB (byte addressable memory). The physical address space is 64 MB. Calculate the size of the segment table (in MB).
questions.solution: Segment table size = 8K pages × 2 KB = 2^13 × 2^11 = 2^24 B = 16 MB (as per the DPP key).

questions.title: LRU Page Faults
questions.question: Given 3 page frames and page references in the order 2, 3, 4, 5, 2, 3, 6, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, using the LRU page replacement algorithm, the number of page faults will be ___.
questions.solution: Faults occur on 2, 3, 4, 5, 2, 3, 6, 4, 5, 6 and hits only on the 8th and 9th references: 10 faults. (The printed DPP key shows 9, which is the FIFO count for this string.)

questions.title: Virtual Memory Policies
questions.question: Which of the following are virtual memory policies?
questions.solution: The OS decides page selection (when to bring a page in) and page replacement (what to replace).

questions.title: FIFO vs LRU (4 Frames)
questions.question: Suppose there are 4 frames in memory and consider the reference string A, B, E, D, C, E, F, A, G, E, D, C, A, C, B. Which of the following is correct?
options: FIFO has fewer page faults than LRU.
LRU has fewer page faults than FIFO.
Both FIFO and LRU have equal page faults.
questions.solution: FIFO gives 13 page faults and LRU gives 12, so LRU has fewer.

questions.title: EMAT with Page Faults
questions.question: Consider a system with a page fault service time of 158 ns and a page hit ratio of 75%. If the memory access time is 10 ns, then the effective memory access time (EMAT) is ___ ns.

questions.title: FIFO vs LRU (5 Frames)
questions.question: Consider a main memory with five page frames and the page reference sequence 4, 9, 3, 4, 10, 2, 7, 4, 9, 10, 4, 7, 3, 2, 4. Which statement is true with respect to FIFO and LRU?
options: Page faults in FIFO are more than LRU.
Page faults in LRU are more than FIFO.
Both LRU and FIFO have the same number of page faults.
Page faults in FIFO are 2 more than LRU.
questions.solution: Both FIFO and LRU give 9 page faults for this sequence.

questions.title: Belady's Phenomenon
questions.question: Belady's phenomenon is commonly experienced in:
questions.solution: Belady's anomaly cannot occur in stack algorithms like LRU and optimal, but can occur in FIFO, second chance and random replacement.

questions.title: Optimal Page Faults (4 Frames)
questions.question: Given the page reference string 1, 10, 1, 2, 9, 2, 9, 8, 9, 8, 2, 3, 9, 3, 8, 9, 3, 4, 9, 3 and 4 page frames, how many page faults will occur with the optimal page replacement policy?
questions.solution: Faults occur for 1, 10, 2, 9, 8, 3 and 4 (7 in total).

questions.title: Optimal Page Faults (3 Frames)
questions.question: Given 3 page frames and page references in the order 2, 3, 4, 5, 2, 3, 6, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, using the optimal page replacement algorithm, the number of page faults will be ___.
questions.solution: Optimal replacement evicts the page used farthest in the future, giving 7 page faults.

questions.title: Virtual Page and Offset
questions.question: A 32-bit address system uses paged virtual memory with a page size of 2 KB. What are the virtual page number and the offset (in decimal) for the virtual address 0x00030f40 respectively?
questions.solution: Offset = 11 bits. Page number = 0x30f40 >> 11 = 0x61 = 97 and offset = 0x740 = 1856.

questions.title: Maximum and Minimum Page Faults
questions.question: Suppose a page-reference string for a process with x frames (initially all empty) has length s, and y distinct page numbers occur in it. (i) What is the maximum number of page faults? (ii) What is the minimum number of page faults?
questions.solution: The maximum is every reference faulting (s) and the minimum is one fault per distinct page (y).

questions.title: Page Faults by Page Hits (MRU)
questions.question: If MRU is used as the page replacement policy with four initially empty page frames for the reference string 4 2 5 1 3 5 6 2 3 2 3 4 5 2 3, what is the value of (number of page faults) / (number of page hits)? (Round off to 3 decimals.)
questions.solution: With MRU: faults on 4, 2, 5, 1, 3, 6 and 5 (7 faults) and 8 hits, so 7/8 = 0.875. (The printed DPP key shows 4, using 12 faults and 3 hits.)

questions.title: EMAT with LRU Hit Ratio
questions.question: Consider a system with 3 frames using the LRU page replacement policy for the page reference string 3 2 3 4 1 4 2 4 1 2. What will be the effective memory access time (in ns) if the TLB access time is 30 ns and the main memory access time is 90 ns?
questions.solution: With 3 frames LRU gives 5 faults and 5 hits, so the hit ratio is 0.5. EMAT = 0.5 × (30 + 90) + 0.5 × (30 + 90 + 90) = 60 + 105 = 165 ns. (The printed key shows 156, which corresponds to 4 frames, i.e. a hit ratio of 0.6.)

questions.title: When Does a Page Fault Occur
questions.question: When will a page fault occur?
options: When a process tries to access a page which is not in the CPU.
When a process tries to access a page which is not on disk.
When a process tries to access a page which is not in main memory.
questions.solution: A page fault occurs when the referenced page is not present in main memory.

questions.title: Reference String from Addresses
questions.question: Consider the following virtual addresses: 784, 224, 634, 734, 546, 978, 444, 299, 712, 526. If the page size is 150 bytes, then the reference string will be:
questions.solution: Page number = ⌊address / 150⌋: 5, 1, 4, 4, 3, 6, 2, 1, 4, 3. Consecutive repeats are merged, giving 5, 1, 4, 3, 6, 2, 1, 4, 3.

questions.title: Length of Reference String plus Unique Pages
questions.question: Consider the virtual addresses 709, 540, 612, 311, 456, 908, 806, 708, 580, 250, 412. If the page size is 200 B, what is the sum of the length of the corresponding reference string and the number of unique pages in it?
questions.solution: Pages: 3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 4, 3, 2, 1, 2. Merging consecutive repeats gives 3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3, 2, 1, 2 (length 10) with 4 unique pages. Sum = 10 + 4 = 14.

questions.title: Excessive Paging
questions.question: Excessive paging activity results in ___.
questions.solution: Excessive paging activity (high page fault rate) is called thrashing.

questions.title: Thrashing Statements
questions.question: Which of the following statements are correct?
options: High thrashing can lead to deadlock.
Lack of frames in main memory causes thrashing.
Increasing memory frames can reduce page faults.
A high degree of multiprogramming can cause poor throughput.
questions.solution: As per the DPP key, all four statements are correct.

questions.title: Minimum Page Demand (Working Set)
questions.question: If the size of the working set window (Δ) for a set of pages is 4 and the page reference string is 5, 4, 3, 1, 5, 4, 5, 3, 4, 5, what could be the minimum page demand of the process at any time?
questions.solution: Counting distinct pages in each window of 4 references: 4, 4, 4, 3, 3, 3, 3. The minimum is 3.

questions.title: Handling Thrashing
questions.question: Which of the following techniques is/are used to handle thrashing and make the system thrashing-free?
questions.solution: The working set model and controlling the page fault frequency are the techniques used to handle thrashing.

questions.title: Working Set (t, k)
questions.question: The working set (t, k) at an instant of time t is:
options: The set of k references with high frequency
The set of k future references that the OS will make in the next t units of time
The set of k pages that have been referenced in the last t time units
questions.solution: Working set at time t is the set of pages referenced in the last k (window) time units, as per the DPP key.

questions.title: Cluster in a Disk
questions.question: What is a cluster in a disk architecture?
options: It is a group of one or more sectors on the same track.
It is a collection of tracks on the same cylinder.
It is a group of one or more tracks on the same platter.
It is a collection of platters on the disk.
questions.solution: A cluster is a group of one or more sectors on the same track.

questions.title: Unformatted Disk Capacity
questions.question: Consider the following disk specifications: number of platters = 8, number of tracks per surface = 512, number of sectors per track = 4096, sector offset = 15 bits. Calculate the unformatted capacity (in GB).
questions.solution: Sector size = 2^15 B = 32 KB. Capacity = 8 × 512 × 4096 × 32 KB = 2^3 × 2^9 × 2^12 × 2^15 B = 2^39 B = 512 GB (as per the DPP key).

questions.title: Disk Data Rate
questions.question: In a computer system, a disk track can hold 32 sectors, each of size 256 bytes. The rotation rate is 2000 rpm. The data rate of the disk is ___ KB per second (approximately).
questions.solution: Track capacity = 32 × 256 B = 8192 B. Rotations per second = 2000/60. Data rate = 8192 × 2000/60 ≈ 273 KB/s.

questions.title: Time to Read a Sector
questions.question: A disk rotates at 7200 RPM. It has 500 sectors of 512 bytes each around the outer cylinder. How long does it take to read a sector?
questions.solution: One rotation = 60/7200 s = 8.33 ms and reads all 500 sectors. Time per sector = 8.33 ms / 500 = 16.67 µs.

questions.title: Average Service Time
questions.question: Consider a 10 GB disk rotating at 10,000 rpm, data transfer rate 10^7 bytes/sec, average seek time 8 ms and block size 32 KB. What is the average service time to access a single disk block from a random location on the disk?
questions.solution: Seek = 8 ms. Average rotational latency = ½ × 6 ms = 3 ms. Transfer time = 32 × 1024 / 10^7 = 3.28 ms. Total = 14.28 ms.

questions.title: Total Swap Time
questions.question: A hard disk has 20 surfaces with 100 tracks per surface and 16 sectors per track. The disk transfer rate is 10^6 bytes/sec, page size is 512 bytes, the process size is 2048 bytes, and the seek time is 25 ms. The disk rotates at 3000 rpm. What is the total swap time (in ms, up to three decimal places)? (The source text printed 300 rpm; the worked solution uses 3000 rpm.)
questions.solution: One rotation = 20 ms, so average rotational latency = 10 ms. Transfer time of 2048 B = 2.048 ms. Swap time = 2 × (25 + 10 + 2.048) = 74.096 ms. (The printed DPP key shows 70.096, which does not match its own working.)

questions.title: Average Read/Write Time
questions.question: Consider a disk that rotates at 20000 RPM with a transfer rate of 32 kBps. If the average seek time is 6 ms and the controller's transfer time is twice the disk transfer time, the average time needed to read or write a 1024-byte sector is ___ ms (up to 1 decimal place).
questions.solution: Rotation time = 3 ms, so average rotational latency = 1.5 ms. Disk transfer time = 1024/(32 × 1024) s = 32 ms; controller transfer time = 64 ms. Total = 6 + 1.5 + 32 + 64 = 103.5 ms.

questions.title: Steps to Use a Disk
questions.question: Two steps performed by the operating system to use a disk to hold its files are:
questions.solution: The OS partitions the disk into one or more groups of cylinders and then performs logical formatting (creates the file system).

questions.title: SCAN Head Movement
questions.question: Consider a disk queue with I/O requests to blocks on cylinders 53, 98, 140, 59, 115, 185, 197, 86. The SCAN algorithm is used. The head is initially at 100 moving towards the left. The cylinders are numbered 0 to 199. The total head movement incurred while servicing these requests is ___.
questions.solution: Moving left: 100 → 98 → 86 → 59 → 53 → 0 = 100. Then 0 → 115 → 140 → 185 → 197 = 197 more. Total = 100 + 197 = 299 (head goes to 0 before reversing).

questions.title: Incorrect Statements about Disk and CPU
questions.question: Consider the statements: S1: Loop instructions cannot be interrupted till they complete. S2: Nearest cylinder next disk scheduling gives the best throughput in comparison to FCFS. S3: Using a large file block size in a fixed block size file system leads to poor disk throughput. Which of the above statements are incorrect?
questions.solution: S1 is false: the CPU checks for interrupts after each instruction, so a loop can be interrupted. S2 is true (SSTF has better throughput but may starve). S3 is false: a larger block gives better throughput but poorer space utilization.

questions.title: SSTF Service Order
questions.question: Consider a disk with cylinders numbered 0 to 99. The disk arm is at cylinder 40 and the queue of disk requests is for cylinders 16, 35, 25, 60, 80, 90 and 20. If Shortest Seek Time First (SSTF) is used, the request for cylinder 60 is serviced after servicing ___ requests.
questions.solution: SSTF order from 40: 35, 25, 20, 16, then 60, 80, 90. So 60 is serviced after 4 requests.

questions.title: Maximum File Size (I-node)
questions.question: A UNIX-style i-node has 10 direct pointers, two single, 5 double and 2 triple indirect pointers. The disk block size is 8 KB and a disk block address is 32 bits. The maximum possible file size is ___ TB (approximately).
questions.solution: Pointers per block = 8 KB / 4 B = 2^11. The two triple-indirect pointers dominate: 2 × (2^11)^3 × 2^13 B = 2^47 B = 128 TB.

questions.title: C-LOOK Total Time
questions.question: Consider a disk queue with request sequence 125, 85, 46, 74, 80, 112, 21, 53, 140. The initial head position is 50 and it is moving towards the right. The cylinders are numbered 0 to 150. Calculate the total time (in ms) required to serve these requests if 4 ms are needed to move the head from one cylinder to another and C-LOOK is used.
questions.solution: Head movement: 50 → 140 = 90, jump 140 → 21 = 119, then 21 → 46 = 25. Total = 234 cylinders. Time = 234 × 4 = 936 ms.

questions.title: File and Record Statements
questions.question: Choose the correct statements from the following.
options: A record is a collection of related fields that can be treated as a unit by some application program.
A file is a collection of similar records.
A database is a collection of non-related data.
A field is the basic element of data.
questions.solution: A database is a collection of related data, so (c) is incorrect.

questions.title: Maximum File Size (6 direct, 4 single, 3 double)
questions.question: Each inode in a file system has 6 direct pointers, 4 single-indirect pointers and 3 double-indirect pointers. A disk block is 500 bytes and a pointer to a disk block is 10 bytes. The entire disk consists of at most 17,000,000 bytes. Calculate the maximum size (in bytes) of a file in this file system.

questions.title: Maximum File Size (UNIX, 512-bit Blocks)
questions.question: In a UNIX OS, each data block is 512 bits and each node has 5 direct data block addresses and three additional addresses: one for a single indirect block, one for a double indirect block and one for a triple indirect block. Each block is addressed with 128 bits. Calculate the maximum size of a file possible in the file system (in k-bits).
questions.solution: Pointers per block = 512/128 = 4. Blocks = 5 + 4 + 4² + 4³ = 89. Size = 89 × 512 = 45,568 bits ≈ 45.568 k-bits, which matches none of the given ranges.

questions.title: Total New Processes (switch with fork)
questions.question: Consider the code: #include<stdio.h> int main() { int i; for (i = 0; i < 5; i += 2) { switch(i) { case 0: fork(); case 1: fork(); fork(); case 2: fork(); fork(); break; case 3: fork(); fork(); fork(); break; case 4: for (j = i; j >= 1; j--) fork(); } } return 0; } What will be the number of child (newly created) processes for the above code?
questions.solution: The cases fall through. i = 0 executes 5 forks (case 0, case 1 and case 2), i = 2 executes 2 forks (case 2) and i = 4 executes 4 forks (case 4). Total forks = 11, so processes = 2^11 = 2048 and new processes = 2047.

questions.title: Child Processes from for Loop
questions.question: Consider the code: main() { for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) fork(); }. How many child (newly created) processes are created?
questions.solution: n sequential fork() calls create 2^n processes, so 2^5 − 1 = 31 new processes.

questions.title: Match Scheduling Terms
questions.question: Match List-I and List-II. List-I: A. Context switching, B. Degree of multiprogramming, C. Message passing, D. Fork(). List-II: 1. Process creation, 2. Dispatcher, 3. Long term scheduler, 4. Inter process communication.
questions.solution: Context switching → dispatcher; degree of multiprogramming → long-term scheduler; message passing → IPC; fork() → process creation.

questions.title: Interface to OS Services
questions.question: To access the services of the operating system, the interface is provided by the ___.
questions.solution: System calls provide the interface to the services of the operating system.

questions.title: Output Count of fork()
questions.question: The following program fragment prints the string "GATE2023" how many times? main() { fork(); fork(); printf("GATE2023\n"); }
questions.solution: Two forks create 2^2 = 4 processes and each prints the string once.

questions.title: Thread Library Scheduling
questions.question: Which of the following scheduling can be done by the thread library?
questions.solution: A user-level thread library schedules user threads; the kernel schedules processes and kernel threads.

questions.title: Child Processes (k loop)
questions.question: Consider the code: void main() { for (int k = 1; k < 5; k++) pid[k] = fork(); }. How many child processes are created by the above code?
questions.solution: The loop runs 4 times, creating 2^4 − 1 = 15 child processes.

questions.title: User vs Kernel Threads
questions.question: Consider the statements about user-level and kernel-level threads: S1: Context switching in kernel-level threads is faster than in user-level threads. S2: If one user-level thread gets blocked, the entire process also gets blocked. S3: Kernel-level threads can be scheduled independently.
questions.solution: User-level thread switching is faster (S1 false). Blocking of one user-level thread blocks the process (S2) and kernel threads are scheduled independently (S3).

questions.title: Types of System Calls
questions.question: What are the types of system calls in an operating system?
questions.solution: System calls are grouped into process control, file management, device management, information maintenance and communication.

questions.title: Kernel Mode Operations
questions.question: Which of the following operations requires the executing code to be operating in kernel mode?
questions.solution: As per the DPP key, disabling interrupts is a privileged operation that needs kernel mode.
